authorial_core.baseline_prompt_en: An environmental photograph of Flintlock Fantasy: a distinct everyday episode in which gunpowder-era technology and a physical magical effect share one working space. The central figure is a woman guided by the supplied portrait, preserving the reference facial proportions and short black bob with wispy bangs. Her dark eyes and softly rounded face remain recognizable within the inhabited scene. She is a sail-mender in a small quay workshop, repairing a salt-stiffened red-and-cream signal flag before the next boat leaves. Her left palm presses a square canvas patch flat against the sloping worktable while her right hand draws a needle through the joined cloth at the near edge of the patch, the loose thread visibly joining that hand to the new stitch. A brass clamp hovers above the far corner of the table, gripping the flag's opposite edge; a clear band of empty air separates its lower jaw from the tabletop, and a restrained blue light follows the engraved grooves in its brass. The lifted flag edge creates a shallow taut fold toward the patch, connecting the impossible tool to the actual repair. She has paused to look toward the waiting dock sentry, with a small amused half-smile and relaxed shoulders; an intimate warmth of expression quietly carries her presence. The sentry at camera-right holds a wood-stock flintlock musket diagonally across his coat, its external cock, frizzen and pan turned toward the viewer in the same focus zone as the worktable. His free hand rests on a weathered rope bale, visibly waiting for the flag rather than interrupting her work. A plain linen shirt with rolled sleeves, faded blue waistcoat and worn apron belong to the workday. Behind them, an open workshop door reveals the low stone quay, moored sailing masts and pale morning water. Frame from just below the tabletop to a little above their heads with the mender dominant left of center, her face, needle contact, hovering clamp and musket lock arranged as four readable points of one scene. Soft harbor daylight from the doorway gives skin, thread and scarred brass tangible texture; cool water reflections stay subordinate to the warm face and red cloth. Use plausible photographic perspective and enough depth of field to connect both people with their tools.
